questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: How many pairs of synovial articulations are associated with the exterior of the skull?
questions.explanation: There are 2 pairs of synovial articulations that are associated with the exterior of the skull. They are the temporomandibular joint and the lateral joints (part of the atlantooccipital joints). Joints of the cranial vault include fibrous joints (sutures), which facilitate growth of the skull and account for the majority of skull joints; primary cartilaginous joints, present between two bones in the skull base; and synovial joints, including the temporomandibular joints and atlantooccipital joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which skull bone is known as Inca?
questions.explanation: The interparietal bone of the skull is known as the Inca bone. It is a sutural bone that lies between the occipital and the parietal bones. Sutural or Wormian bones are islands of bone commonly found within the lambdoid suture in some individuals. They may arise from separate centres of ossification and usually have no clinical significance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While counselling the parents of a baby with anterior plagiocephaly, you explain that one of the skull sutures has prematurely fused. The affected suture is present between:
questions.explanation: In anterior plagiocephaly, premature fusion of the coronal suture is seen. The coronal suture is present between the frontal and parietal bones. Major sutures of the skull are: lambdoid suture - between parietal and occipital bones; sagittal suture - between the two parietal bones; metopic suture - between the two frontal bones. Craniosynostosis is congenital premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, resulting in an abnormal head shape.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presenting with right-sided shoulder droop and an absent gag reflex was diagnosed with Vernet's syndrome. Which of the following structures passes through the posterior part of the involved foramen?
questions.explanation: Vernet's syndrome or jugular foramen syndrome refers to palsies of the IX, X and XI cranial nerves traversing the jugular foramen. The sigmoid sinus passes through the posterior aspect of the jugular foramen. The jugular foramen can be divided into three compartments: anterior - inferior petrosal sinus; intermediate - CN IX, X and XI; posterior - sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein. Arteries passing through include the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery and the meningeal branch of the occipital artery; emissary veins may also traverse it.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the structure passing through the foramen marked.
questions.explanation: The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure and the abducens nerve passes through it. The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve and arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction. It runs through Dorello's canal at the medial end of the petrous ridge, enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery, then enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring and supplies the lateral rectus. Other options: the spinal accessory nerve passes through the foramen magnum; the ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal with the optic nerve; the middle meningeal artery and vein pass through the foramen spinosum with the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ER after receiving a punch to the right side of his face. His X-ray is shown below. Which of the following bones maximally contributes to the region fractured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a fracture of the floor of the orbit. The maxilla makes the maximum contribution to the floor of the orbit. The source lists the boundaries and constituent bones of the bony orbit: the roof is formed principally by the orbital plate of the frontal bone with the lesser wing of sphenoid posteriorly; the floor includes the orbital plate of maxilla, zygomatic bone and orbital process of palatine bone; the medial wall includes maxilla, lacrimal bone, ethmoid bone and sphenoid; and the lateral wall includes zygomatic bone and greater wing of sphenoid. The orbital floor can fracture after trauma to the orbit, with orbital contents herniating into the maxillary sinus and producing a teardrop-like appearance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following bony structures is present behind the marked area?
questions.explanation: The structure marked in the image is the pterion, and the bony structure present behind it is the lesser wing of the sphenoid. The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull: frontal bone, squamous part of the temporal bone, greater wing of sphenoid bone and parietal bone. The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery lies deep to it. It also overlies the lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere, so a hematoma can cause compressive lesions there.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While resecting an acoustic neuroma via the middle cranial fossa approach, the surgeon drills over the arcuate eminence of the petrous temporal bone. What is the inferior relation of the structure being drilled?
questions.explanation: The superior semicircular canal is present beneath the arcuate eminence of the petrous temporal bone. The arcuate eminence is used as a neurosurgical landmark for the superior semicircular canal in surgeries done by the middle cranial fossa approach. The temporal bone consists of squamous, mastoid, petrous and tympanic parts, as well as the styloid and zygomatic processes. The petrous temporal bone is a pyramid-shaped structure. Its relations include: inferior to the arcuate eminence - superior semicircular canal; posterior surface - internal auditory meatus and vestibular aqueduct; inferior surface - carotid canal and jugular fossa (jugular notch).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 2 week-old neonate developed meningitis following a scalp abscess. What is the likely route of spread?
questions.explanation: The infection has likely spread from the sub-aponeurotic tissue. The sub-aponeurotic loose areolar tissue of the scalp is referred to as the dangerous area of the scalp. Infection from this layer can pass into the cranial cavity through small emissary veins, which pass through parietal foramina in the calvaria. It can reach intracranial structures causing meningitis and intracranial abscesses. The scalp consists of 5 layers (mnemonic - SCALP): skin; connective tissue; aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle; loose areolar (sub-aponeurotic) tissue; and pericranium.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man was brought to the emergency with a profusely bleeding scalp laceration following a road traffic accident. What is the nature and layer of origin of the bleed?
questions.explanation: Scalp bleeding is predominantly arterial, from the dense connective tissue of the scalp. Profuse bleeding from scalp injuries occurs because of low venous pressure in the erect posture and because the dense connective tissue holds the arteries open and does not allow them to retract, causing profuse bleeding. The scalp has an extremely rich blood supply from branches of the external carotid arteries. Profuse bleeding from a scalp laceration requires rapid control by sutures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is unlikely to be involved in a patient with Bell's palsy?
questions.explanation: The motor component of levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor (III cranial) nerve and the smooth muscle component is innervated by sympathetic nerves. It is uninvolved in Bell's palsy. All the other listed facial muscles are innervated by the facial nerve and therefore can be paralyzed in Bell's palsy.

questions.question: Match the following muscles of facial expression with their actions.
questions.explanation: The source lists examples of muscles of facial expression and their actions: orbicularis oculi - closing eyelids; risorius - retracts the angle of the mouth (grinning muscle); orbicularis oris - closes mouth; mentalis - wrinkles chin; corrugator supercilii - frowning; zygomaticus major - smiling and laughing; depressor anguli oris - depresses angle of mouth; levator labii superioris - elevates upper lip; depressor labii inferioris - depresses lower lip; buccinator - known as the whistling muscle and flattens the cheeks against the gums and teeth. Note: modiolus is a fibromuscular structure formed by the interlacing of 5 muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following muscles plays a role in winking?
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle plays a role in winking. It is a broad, flat, elliptical circumorbital muscle surrounding the circumference of the orbit and spreading into adjacent regions. It has orbital, palpebral and lacrimal parts and plays an important role in facial expression and ocular reflexes; it mainly closes the eyelids. It is supplied by branches of the facial, superficial temporal, maxillary and ophthalmic arteries and innervated by the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with a loss of sensation over the marked area. Which nerve may be damaged?
questions.explanation: The skin over the angle of the mandible is innervated by the great auricular nerve. Most of the skin covering the face is innervated solely by branches of the trigeminal nerve except the skin over the angle of the mandible, which is supplied by the great auricular nerve from the C2 cervical plexus, and the ear, which also receives supply from the vagus nerve, facial nerve and cervical plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While testing the cranial nerves in a stroke patient, you ask her to try to whistle. Which of the following structures doesn't pierce the muscle responsible for this action?

options.text: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Buccal branch of the mandibular nerve

questions.correctAnswerText: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is involved in flattening the cheeks against the gums and teeth; hence it is known as the whistling muscle. The buccal branch of the facial nerve innervates the buccinator muscle but does not pierce it. Structures piercing the buccinator muscle are: parotid duct; buccal branch of the mandibular nerve; and molar mucous glands which lie on the buccopharyngeal fascia around the parotid duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nerves is related to Dorello's canal?
questions.explanation: The abducens nerve is related to Dorello's canal. The abducens nerve enters the cavernous sinus by passing within this canal. Dorello's canal is an interdural space limited superiorly by the petrosphenoidal ligament, laterally by the petrous apex, and medially by the dorsum sellae. This is a confluence of superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, cavernous sinus and basilar plexus venous sinuses. Dorello's canal anatomy is clinically significant in understanding sixth-nerve palsy and in skull-base surgery, especially for petroclival lesions.
